definition: Acting suddenly on a feeling or wish without stopping to think first.
example: In an impulsive moment, he signed up for a pottery class he had never heard of before that morning.
nuance: Impulsive stresses acting before thinking and often hints at regret; spontaneous is gentler and usually praises an unplanned choice.
prompt: A teenager walks past a shop window on the way home from school.
options: Maya made an impulsive decision to spend her bus fare on a hat in the window.
Maya was impulsive, so she compared prices at six shops over a month before buying.
Being impulsive, Maya had to touch the glass exactly four times before she could walk on.
The impulsive display, with its glittering lights, made Maya stop and stare in awe.
reasons: Spending money she needed, on the spot and without weighing it, is acting on a sudden urge.
A month of careful comparison is planned behavior, the reverse of acting on a whim.
A repeated ritual someone feels driven to perform is compulsive, not a sudden one-time urge.
This confuses the word with impressive; a window display cannot act without thinking.

practice.prompt: A group of friends is getting ready for a weekend camping trip.
options: Jonah was impulsive about going because his parents ordered him to attend.
Jonah's impulsive suggestion to leave at midnight meant nobody remembered to pack the tent.
Jonah was impulsive, writing a checklist and studying the weather forecast every day for weeks.
The impulsive smell of the old sleeping bag made everyone hold their noses.
reasons: Doing something because others require it is obligation, not acting on one's own sudden urge.
Rushing off on a sudden idea, with no time to plan, led to a forgotten essential.
Weeks of steady preparation show forethought, which is the opposite of the word's meaning.
This mixes the word up with repulsive; a smell can be disgusting but cannot act rashly.
